hints: Think about what any electrode potential must be measured against, since a single half cell voltage cannot be measured alone.
Recall the three standard condition values for ion concentration, gas pressure and temperature that make the $E$ value a standard $E^{\ominus}$ value.
walkthrough:
See why a reference is essential**
You can never dip a voltmeter into one beaker and read an absolute half cell potential. A voltage is always a difference between two electrodes. By international agreement all half cells are compared to the standard hydrogen electrode, which is given $E^{\ominus} = 0.00\ \text{V}$. So your definition must say compared to SHE.

Add the three standard conditions**
The $\ominus$ sign means everything is in its standard state. For solutions that is $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for all aqueous ions. For any gas it is $101\ \text{kPa}$. For everything it is $298\ \text{K}$. Miss one and you lose the second mark, so learn the trio together.

Final answer: The e.m.f. / voltage of a half cell compared to / connected to the standard hydrogen electrode.
Under standard conditions of $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ for ions, $101\ \text{kPa}$ for gases and $298\ \text{K}$.

hints: Picture the two half cells side by side, the left side must be the hydrogen reference and the right side the silver test electrode.
Remember what metal is needed for each electrode, especially when the half cell has no solid metal of its own.
Think how the two solutions are connected electrically without mixing, and how the voltage is read without drawing current.
walkthrough:
Build the silver half cell on the right**
This is the simple side. Dip a silver rod or foil, $\text{Ag(s)}$, into a solution containing $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})$, for example $\text{AgNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$. The equilibrium is $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$, so you have both the ion and the metal present.

Build the hydrogen reference on the left**
The hydrogen half cell has no metal of its own, so you need inert platinum to conduct electrons. Bubble $\text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$ over the Pt foil dipping into $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$, for example $\text{HCl(aq)}$. Label the gas supply, the Pt, $\text{H}_{2}$ and $\text{H}^{+}$. That gives $2\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$.

Complete the circuit correctly**
Join the two solutions with a salt bridge, usually filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$, to allow ion flow. Join the two metals with wires through a high resistance voltmeter. Draw Pt wired to voltmeter wired to Ag. That complete loop lets you read $E^{\ominus}$ for $\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}$.

Final answer: Left beaker: Pt electrode in $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$ with $\text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$ bubbled over Pt via gas inlet.
Right beaker: Ag electrode in $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq})$.
Two beakers linked by salt bridge, electrodes joined by wires to a voltmeter, Pt to voltmeter to Ag.

hints: Write the reduction equilibrium $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$ and ask which way it shifts if $\text{Ag}^{+}$ is removed.
walkthrough:
Use Le Chatelier on the half equation**
Sit with $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$. Lowering $[\text{Ag}^{+}]$ removes reactant, so the system opposes the change by shifting left to make more $\text{Ag}^{+}$. Reduction becomes less favoured, electrons are less readily accepted, so the electrode potential drops and becomes more negative than $E^{\ominus}$.
Final answer: $E$ becomes more negative / less positive, as $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)}$ shifts to the left.

hints: Focus on the mole scale and the starting and finishing states, solid solute plus water going to aqueous ions.
walkthrough:
Pin down per mole and dissolve**
Think of tipping one mole of solid into excess water until it disappears to give $\text{aq}$ ions. The heat absorbed or released in that exact process, $\text{solid} + \text{aq} \rightarrow \text{aqueous solution}$, is $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^{\ominus}$. Always quote one mole of solute.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of solute dissolves in water / to form aqueous solution.

hints: Place the three energy levels in order, gaseous ions at the top, aqueous ions in the middle, solid at the bottom, and think which arrow is hydration.
Check that every species carries a correct state symbol, $(\text{g})$, $(\text{s})$ or $(\text{aq})$, and that charges balance.
walkthrough:
Label the levels with states**
Start at the top with fully separated gas ions, $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{g}) + \text{NO}_{3}^{-}(\text{g})$. Going down with water gives hydrated ions, $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$. At the bottom put the solid, $\text{AgNO}_{3}(\text{s})$. State symbols are essential, $(\text{g})$ versus $(\text{aq})$ tells the examiner which step is which.

Insert arrows to close the Hess triangle**
Draw a downward arrow from gaseous ions to aqueous ions for hydration, $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}^{\ominus}$. Draw a downward arrow from gaseous ions to solid for lattice formation, $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus}$. The solid to aqueous route is $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^{\ominus}$. By Hess, solution = reverse of lattice formation + hydration.

Final answer: Top level: $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{g}) + \text{NO}_{3}^{-}(\text{g})$
Middle level: $\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{NO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$
Bottom level: $\text{AgNO}_{3}(\text{s})$
Downward arrow top to middle = sum of hydration enthalpies, downward arrow top to bottom = lattice formation, upward / connecting arrow bottom to middle = enthalpy of solution.

hints: Write the Hess expression $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^{\ominus} = -\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus} + \Sigma \Delta H_{\text{hyd}}^{\ominus}$ and rearrange for lattice formation.
walkthrough:
Apply Hess and solve**
Dissolving is solid to aqueous. Imagine solid to gas (reverse of formation) then gas to aqueous: $$\Delta H_{\text{sol}}^{\ominus} = -\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus} + \Delta H_{\text{hyd}}^{\ominus}(\text{Ag}^{+}) + \Delta H_{\text{hyd}}^{\ominus}(\text{NO}_{3}^{-})$$ Put numbers in: $$+22.6 = -\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus} + (-475) + (-314)$$ So $$-\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus} = +22.6 + 789 = +811.6$$ Hence for formation, gaseous to solid, $$\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus} = -811.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Order the three solids from most exothermic to least exothermic by comparing the cation charges first.
For the two $1+$ cations, compare the sizes of $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Rb}^{+}$ and recall how distance affects attraction.
Link charge and size to the strength of attraction between oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
walkthrough:
Rank by charge first**
Lattice energy is driven by attraction of $+$ to $-$. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ carries double the charge of $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Rb}^{+}$, so it pulls $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ far more strongly. Put $\text{Mg(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}(\text{s})$ as most exothermic / largest magnitude without hesitation.

Split Na and Rb by size**
Both are $1+$, so look at radius. $\text{Na}^{+}$ is in Period 3, $\text{Rb}^{+}$ is in Period 5, so $\text{Na}^{+}$ is much smaller. A smaller ion lets the centres of $+$ and $-$ get closer, and electrostatic force rises sharply as distance falls. So $\text{NaNO}_{3}(\text{s})$ is more exothermic than $\text{RbNO}_{3}(\text{s})$.

State the electrostatic reason**
Tie it together: magnitude of $\Delta H_{\text{latt}}^{\ominus}$ increases with increasing ionic charge and decreasing ionic radius because the attraction between oppositely charged ions is stronger, ionic bonding is stronger, and more energy is released when the lattice forms from gaseous ions.

Final answer: Most exothermic $\text{Mg(NO}_{3}\text{)}_{2}(\text{s})$, then $\text{NaNO}_{3}(\text{s})$, least exothermic $\text{RbNO}_{3}(\text{s})$.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has higher charge than $\text{Na}^{+}$ / $\text{Rb}^{+}$ and $\text{Na}^{+}$ is smaller than $\text{Rb}^{+}$.
Greater charge and smaller radius give stronger attraction between ions / stronger ionic bonds, so more exothermic lattice energy.
